title: Obadiah 1:15–18
context: The LORD declares that the day of the LORD is near on all the nations, and he states a principle: as you have done, it will be done to you, and your deeds will return on your own head (compare Joel 3:7; Ezekiel 35:15). He says that as you have drunk on his holy mountain, so the nations will drink continually; interpreters differ on whether you here refers to Edom celebrating on Zion or to Judah, which drank the cup of judgment (compare Jeremiah 25:15, 28; Isaiah 51:17). On Mount Zion there will be those who escape, and it will be holy (compare Joel 2:32); the house of Jacob will possess its possessions, and the house of Jacob and the house of Joseph will be a fire, with the house of Esau as stubble, so that none of Esau remains. The section ends, Indeed, the LORD has spoken. Readers take the day of the LORD here in historic, typological, and future senses, and these readings appear in both traditions. Shared ground: Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat God’s just judgment of the nations, the reversal of Edom’s deeds, and the preservation of a holy remnant on Zion as common confession.

verses.text: For the day of the LORD is near all the nations! As you have done, it will be done to you. Your deeds will return upon your own head.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the day of the LORD near on all nations, and the principle that as you have done, it will be done to you. Deeds return on the doer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s just repayment (compare Galatians 6:7; Matthew 7:2). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the day of the LORD and this principle as common confession, whatever view a reader takes of the millennium.

verses.text: For as you have drunk on my holy mountain, so all the nations will drink continually. Yes, they will drink, swallow down, and will be as though they had not been.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the image of drinking on God’s holy mountain and the nations drinking continually. Judgment will reach all nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cup of God’s judgment (compare Jeremiah 25:15). Shared ground: both traditions generally hold the identity of you in this verse with care, since interpreters read it in more than one way.

verses.text: But in Mount Zion, there will be those who escape, and it will be holy. The house of Jacob will possess their possessions.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see those who escape on Mount Zion, which will be holy, and the house of Jacob possessing its possessions. God preserves a remnant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise of a holy remnant (compare Joel 2:32). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for God’s people after judgment.

verses.text: The house of Jacob will be a fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble. They will burn among them and devour them. There will not be any remaining to the house of Esau.” Indeed, the LORD has spoken.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the house of Jacob and Joseph as fire and the house of Esau as stubble. The reversal of Edom’s cruelty is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the certainty of God’s word, Indeed, the LORD has spoken. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse soberly, as a poetic picture of judgment on Edom.
